rationale: A wins because it knows where the evidence stops. 'Hugging Face says its 1.8B model rivals one four times its size — and the open weights mean anyone can check' turns the benchmark caveat into the story; B's 'Offline AI That Runs on a Laptop Is Now Good Enough for a Fortune 100 Factory' smuggles in a factory use case and adoption claim the facts do not support. B has a few usable angles, but its manufacturer logic is a loaded rake in the hallway.
gaps_in_A: 'Why a Fortune 100 manufacturer signed on early for private model hosting' edges slightly past the supplied facts; the update says the manufacturer is cited as an early enterprise customer, not why it bought or which feature unlocked the deal.

'Hugging Face releases a 1.8B-parameter model built to run offline on a phone or laptop' is valid but launch-shaped; without the hardware and tokens-per-second proof it names, it risks becoming a model-card item, not a story.
gaps_in_B: 'Offline AI That Runs on a Laptop Is Now Good Enough for a Fortune 100 Factory' invents the core story. The facts do not say the manufacturer runs the on-device model, uses it in a factory, or proved it good enough for real workloads.
'a Fortune 100 manufacturer already using it' conflates an early enterprise Hub customer with usage of the offline model. That is not a nuance; that is the part a reporter will fact-check first.

'The Factory That Runs AI Without a Cloud Connection' is unsupported. The update says the model can run offline and names a manufacturer customer; it does not say plant-floor deployment, cloud prohibition, data sovereignty, or supply-chain use.

'Enterprises Can Deploy This AI Without Owing Anyone a Subscription' overstates the Apache 2.0 implication. Self-hosting may avoid API fees, but enterprise deployment can still require hosting, support, compliance tooling, and contracts.
